玻璃音管琴一詞原指玻璃豎琴；1983年由Sascha Reckert發明為調音玻: The term verrophone originally meant the glass harp; in 1983 Sascha Reckert invented it as an instrument of tuned glass tubes. Earlier glass instruments include the glass harmonica and arrangements of ordinary drinking glasses. Because its radiating surface is larger, the verrophone can be louder than the glass harp, and anything written for the glass harmonica can be played on it. The contemporary artist Barry Prophet makes struck glass-tube instruments in the manner of the glockenspiel and the lithophone, and his work Crystal Bones uses his microtonally tuned glass instruments. Notable players include Friedrich Heinrich Kern, Philipp Alexander Marguerre, Sascha Reckert and Sebastian Reckert.
玻璃音管琴主要由經過精心調音的玻璃管組成，每根玻璃管一端開口。玻璃管按半音階從大: The verrophone consists mainly of carefully tuned glass tubes, each open at one end. The tubes are arranged closely in chromatic order from largest to smallest, in a layout modelled on the traditional organ. It is played with a special beater, or by rubbing the open end of a tube directly with a finger to set it vibrating. The supporting structure may be a wooden or metal frame that holds and orders the tubes. The whole design emphasises the resonance of the glass in order to produce a clear, transparent sound.
玻璃音管琴以摩擦一端開放的玻璃管發聲，也可敲擊或以特殊琴槌摩擦；多管緊密排列，能: The verrophone sounds by rubbing glass tubes that are open at one end, and they can also be struck or rubbed with a special mallet; the tubes stand close together, so several can be rubbed at once to make harmony. Its volume is greater than that of some glass instruments in the same family, and it is more dynamic than the earlier instruments made from rows of drinking glasses, because the radiating surface is larger. Its range runs from G3 to F6, and can be extended to D7 with wine glasses.

The verrophone is a European idiophone invented in 1983 by Sascha Reckert, and it belongs among the glass instruments. It is built of tuned glass tubes, open at the end, arranged chromatically by size. It sounds by rubbing the end of a tube, and the tubes can also be struck or rubbed with a special mallet; several stand side by side, so chords can be played at once. It is louder than some glass instruments such as the glass harmonica, with a range of about G3 to F6, extendable to D7 with wine glasses. Players include Sascha Reckert and others, and the repertory written for the glass harmonica can be played on it.
